product.title: Swedish 101 - A1 (English Edition)
product.description: Twenty Assimil-style self-study units that take you from zero to A1 Swedish: short dialogues, word-for-word translations that show how Swedish builds its sentences, grammar notes, vocabulary with an English-friendly pronunciation guide, exercises, and an answer key. Swedish is closer to English than you might think: the verb never changes for the person (no am/is/are, no -s), there is no masculine/feminine gender to memorize, and thousands of words are already familiar from English. Each unit targets one of the spots that actually trip learners up: the article that sticks to the end of the noun, the double definite with adjectives, the five ways to form a plural, the verb that must sit in second place, and sin/sitt/sina, which has no counterpart in English.

blocks.text: Here is some good news before you even turn the first page: **Swedish spelling is honest**. What you see on the page is almost always what comes out of your mouth. Compare that with Danish, which swallows half of its final letters, or French, which writes *beaucoup* to say "boh-koo" — or, for that matter, English, which spells *though*, *through* and *tough* three different ways. Swedish has a dozen or so sound habits — not hundreds — and they all fit into the short pronunciation chapter you are about to read.

The list of things that are **easier than you'd expect** is a long one. Swedish verbs do not change for the person at all — *jag är, du är, han är, vi är, ni är, de är*: one form for everybody. No *am/is/are*, no *-s* tacked on for he and she. Swedish also has no separate progressive form: *jag äter* means "I eat" **and** "I am eating". You will not have to choose between the two — one form covers both, and context does the rest.

You also already have a head start. Swedish and English are close relatives, so thousands of words read themselves the moment you see them: *hus* (house), *bok* (book), *vatten* (water), *hand*, *finger*, *sommar*, *vinter*, *problem*, *student*, *telefon*, *bank*, *hotell*, *bussen*. As an English speaker, you start Swedish with a thousand words for free.

There are difficulties, of course, and this course names them right now so they don't ambush you halfway through. There are four: **the article that sticks to the end of the noun** (*en bok* → *boken*, "the book"), **two noun types** that decide what that ending looks like (*en* and *ett*), **the verb that must sit in second place** in the sentence (*Idag går jag* — not *Idag jag går*), and **five ways to form a plural**. All of them are real, all of them can be counted on one hand, and three of them are wrapped up before Unit 10.

What is *not* on that list is far longer: no masculine and feminine genders to memorize as in French or German; no cases changing the ending of a noun according to its job in the sentence as in Russian or German; no six-line conjugation tables; no tones that change a word's meaning as in Mandarin or Thai. Swedish does have a melody — two word tones, and this course will show you them — but getting the tone wrong in Sweden only makes you sound foreign, it never makes you say the wrong thing.

The dialogues follow **Dian**, an Indonesian student who has just arrived in Stockholm, together with her roommate **Ahmad** and two Swedes in her new life: **Elin**, her neighbor in the Lappis student housing, and **Oskar**, her classmate. What they talk about is deliberately ordinary: looking for keys, buying bread, a packed subway train, afternoon *fika*, a weekend at a red wooden cottage. The language people really use is the language of ordinary things.

Twenty units, one dialogue per unit, about twenty to thirty minutes per sitting. If you do one unit every two days, in six weeks you will reach the last page with enough to open your mouth in Stockholm. *Lycka till* — good luck.

front.title: Contents
front.intro: This course works best in order — each unit reuses what the previous ones put in place.

blocks.text: This course is built for **self-study**. Each unit is designed to be finished in one sitting, about 20-30 minutes. What matters is not how fast you move forward, but how often you come back.
Every unit has the same layout, and the order is deliberate:

items: **Dialogue** — first read the Swedish out loud without looking at the translation. Let your ears do the work before your brain demands an explanation.

**Literal translation** — the small italic line under the translation. This is the part people skip most often, yet it is where you see how Swedish *thinks*. Example: *Jag heter Dian* literally means "I am-called Dian", not "my name is Dian".
**Notes** — short explanations of whatever just felt strange.

**Vocabulary** — the new words of the unit, each with its pronunciation. Nouns are always given with *en* or *ett*, so the noun type sticks from the very first time you see the word. Learning *bok* on its own is not enough; what needs to go in is *en bok*.
**Exercises** — do them without looking at the key. Mistakes are part of the process.
**Answer key** — open it only after you have genuinely tried.

blocks.title: Wave review
items: From Unit 3 on, each unit asks you to revisit an earlier unit — usually two steps back, just the right distance to make your memory work without feeling like starting over. Do it in reverse: cover the Swedish, look at the English translation, and rebuild the Swedish sentence from memory.
This is what turns "I understood it once" into "I can use it". Don't skip it.

blocks.text: One last rule: **say it out loud**. Swedish spelling is honest, but it still has a dozen or so habits you can't see on the page — a *k* that turns into a soft hushing sound, a *g* that becomes *y*, an *o* that sounds like "oo". The "Say it" column in every vocabulary table is not decoration; it is a core part of the lesson. Capital letters mark the stressed syllable: **TAH-lahr** means the stress falls on *ta*.

Read this chapter once now, then come back whenever a word seems to make no sense. No need to memorize it — ninety percent of it will stick on its own through the dialogues. The respellings in this course are written to be read the way an English speaker naturally would: **ah** as in "father" (every Swedish *a*, even at the end of a word: *tala* → **TAH-lah**, *flicka* → **FLIK-kah**), **ee** as in "see", **oo** as in "moon" (only for a Swedish *o* that sounds like "oo"), **oh** as in "go" (but without the glide into "w"), **eh** as in "bed" (also a final *-e*: *kaffe* → **KAHF-feh**), **ay** as in "say", **y** always as in "yes". Two extra symbols, **ü** and **ö**, cover the vowels English doesn't have.
Three extra letters

The Swedish alphabet is the same as the English one, plus three letters at the **very end**: …*x, y, z, å, ä, ö*. They are letters in their own right, not letters with accents — if you look up a word in a dictionary, words starting with *ö* are on the very last pages.

blocks.text: Vowels that fool you

items: **u is not an English "oo".** It sits between "oo" and "ee" — round your lips as if to say "oo", then push your tongue forward as if to say "ee". *hus* → **hüs**, *du* → **dü**, *ute* → **Ü-teh**. This course always writes Swedish *u* as **ü**, long or short — *buss* → **büs**, *student* → **stü-DENT** — and never as "oo".

**y goes even further.** Lips rounded for "oo", tongue as high as for "ee" (like French *u* or German *ü*). *ny* → **nü**, *fyra* → **FÜ-rah**, *tyst* → **tüst**. Also written **ü**; the difference from *u* is small and will never cause a misunderstanding.

**o often sounds like "oo".** This trap catches some of the most common words: *bok* → **boohk** (rhymes with "spook", not "book"), *sova* → **SOO-vah**, *bo* → **boo**, *stor* → **stoor**, *ko* → **koo**. This "oo" sound is the only thing **oo** stands for in this course. Rough rule: a long *o* is usually "oo"; a short *o* before two consonants usually stays a short "o" — *sommar* → **SOM-mahr**, *ost* → **ost**.

**Long and short matter.** A vowel before **one** consonant is long; before **two** consonants it is short. *vit* (white, long vowel) is different from *vitt*; *tak* (roof) is different from *tack* (thanks). When in doubt, go long — Swedes stretch vowels more than English speakers expect.

blocks.text: Two hushing sounds

These are the two sounds that most give a foreigner away, and both show up in very common words. The first is close to English "sh"; the second has no English equivalent at all. Spend five minutes on them now.

blocks.text: If the **hw** sound won't come yet, use a soft, breathy *f* as an emergency exit: *sju* → "fü". Some Swedes say it that way themselves, especially in Skåne. What you must not do is read it "s-yoo" the way it is spelled.

blocks.text: Stress and the two tones

Swedish stress almost always falls on the **first syllable**: **TAH-lahr**, **SKOO-lah**, **VAHT-ten**. Loanwords are the exception, and they usually stress a later syllable: **stü-DENT**, **teh-leh-FOON**, **res-toh-RAHNG**. Throughout this course, capital letters in the "Say it" column mark the stressed syllable.

blocks.title: The tones that make Swedish sound like singing
items: Swedish has **two word tones**. Tone 1 is a simple falling tone, used by one-syllable words and most loanwords. Tone 2 rises, falls and rises again, and is used by most native two-syllable words — that is what makes *tala*, *flicka*, *kaffe* sound like they swing.

Pairs of words that differ only in tone do exist — *anden* can mean "the duck" or "the spirit" — but there are few of them, and context almost always rescues you. **Don't memorize tones one by one.** Listen, imitate, and let them come on their own. A wrong tone will never make you misunderstood.

Personal pronouns
Nouns: two types, four forms
Roughly **three out of four** Swedish nouns are *en*-words. If you really don't know, guess *en* — you'll be right 75% of the time.

blocks.text: Verbs: one form for everybody
The **supine** is the form used with *har* and *hade* — *jag har skrivit*, "I have written". Think of it as the English past participle in "have written": it never stands alone and never changes.
Word order

blocks.title: The verb-second rule, once more
items: In a Swedish statement the verb is **always** the second element. Whatever you put first — a time expression, a place, even a whole subordinate clause — the verb follows right after it, and the subject gets pushed behind the verb.
*Idag går jag hem.* · *På fredag ska vi fika.* · *När jag kommer hem lagar jag mat.*
The only place this rule does not apply is **inside a subordinate clause**, and that is where *inte* moves in front of the verb.

blocks.text: These fifty verbs cover most everyday conversation. The columns: infinitive, present, past, and supine (the form used after *har* and *hade*). Verbs marked **·** are strong verbs — their past forms don't follow a pattern and simply have to be learned, just like English *go – went – gone*.

Notice that the "Present" column has just **one entry** per verb. There is no separate form for *jag*, *du* or *han* — no "I go / she goes" — that is the gift mentioned in the foreword, and it holds for as long as you study Swedish.

You have reached the end of A1. That means you can greet people, introduce yourself, ask what something costs, order food, tell the time, talk about yesterday, and understand short sentences spoken slowly. That is enough to get by for a month in Stockholm. What you don't have yet is speed — and speed only comes with hours of practice.
Three things waiting for you at A2

items: **The passive and *s*-verbs**. *Dörren öppnas klockan nio* ("the door is opened at nine"). The *-s* ending also makes reciprocal verbs: *vi ses* ("see you"), *vi hörs* ("talk soon") — two of the goodbyes you will hear most often.

**Particle verbs** (*partikelverb*). *Ta på sig* (to put on), *tycka om* (to like), *komma ihåg* (to remember), *stänga av* (to turn off). The particle is stressed, and the meaning is often far from the base verb — exactly like *look up* and *give in* in English, so you already know the idea.

**Longer, linked sentences**. At A1 you use *och*, *men*, *att*, *eftersom*. At A2 come *trots att*, *medan*, *innan*, *så att*, *om* — and with them, the subordinate-clause word order you met in Unit 18 becomes something you use every day.

blocks.text: Habits that help more than the next book

items: **Switch on SVT Play or UR Play.** Some of their content is free outside Sweden, and almost every program has Swedish subtitles — not a translation, but subtitles in the same language. Watching with same-language subtitles is the fastest way to connect spelling with sound.

**Look for *lättläst*.** The newspaper *8 Sidor* and the books from *LL-förlaget* are written in simple Swedish for adult readers. That is far more useful than children's books, because the topics are still adult topics.
**Go to a *språkcafé*.** Almost every city library in Sweden runs one for free. If you are not in Sweden yet, there are online versions in many language groups.

**Talk about the same things again and again.** Describe your day in Swedish — alone, out loud, every evening, five sentences. The vocabulary of your own days is the vocabulary you need most, and it only sticks through repetition.

blocks.title: A note about Swedes
items: Almost every Swede speaks excellent English, and they will switch to it the moment they hear you hesitate — even faster if English is clearly your first language. That is not a rejection — it is politeness. But it can stop you from ever making progress.

Your lifesaver sentence: **"Kan vi prata svenska? Jag övar."** — "Can we speak Swedish? I'm practicing." Say it once at the start of a conversation, and almost everyone will happily stay in Swedish with you.

blocks.text: *Tack för att du läste ända hit. Vi hörs!* — Thanks for reading all the way to the end. Talk soon!
